statement:
Implement a sorted multiset: it stores integers, allows duplicates, supports insertion and deletion at any time, and can be read out in ascending order. It must be implemented as a skip list. You may not use "a Python list plus bisect", and you may not use a ready-made sorted container.

A skip list is structured as follows. At the bottom, level 0 is a singly linked list that strings all the nodes together in ascending key order. Each node gets a random height h when it is inserted: start with h = 1, then flip a coin repeatedly, each time increasing h by 1 with probability p (default 1/2), and stop at the first miss; h is also capped at MAX_LEVEL = 32. A node of height h appears on levels 0, 1, ..., h-1, and every level is a linked list sorted by key. On the far left there is a head node head that stores no key and appears on every level.

Keys 3, 7, 12, 19, 25, 31 with heights 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 1:

Level 2   head ----------> 7 -----------------------------------> None
Level 1   head ----------> 7 -----------> 19 -------------------> None
Level 0   head ---> 3 ---> 7 ---> 12 ---> 19 ---> 25 ---> 31 ---> None

A search starts at the top level of head: as long as the key of the node to the right is smaller than the target, move right; otherwise drop down a level. When you can't move any further on level 0, the node to the right is the first node whose key is not less than the target. To find 25 in the picture above: on level 2, go from head to 7; on level 1, go from 7 to 19; on level 0, don't move; the node to the right of 19 is 25. That is 2 steps to the right in total; walking along level 0 alone takes 4 steps.

Sizes and requirements:

  • Keys are integers in [-10**9, 10**9], and there are at most 2 * 10**5 operations in total.
  • Let n be the current number of elements. Every operation must run in expected O(logn) time. The expectation is over the structure's own coin flips, and it must hold for every input order, including inserting in ascending order.
  • The constructor's seed initializes the structure's own random number generator random.Random(seed). It only affects the heights of the internal nodes and must not affect the return value of any operation. p satisfies 0 < p < 1.

Part 1 — Insertion and lookup

class SkipList:
    def __init__(self, seed: int | None = None, p: float = 0.5) -> None: ...
    def add(self, key: int) -> None: ...            # duplicates are kept
    def __contains__(self, key: int) -> bool: ...   # `key in sl`
    def __len__(self) -> int: ...                   # number of stored keys, duplicates counted
    def __iter__(self): ...                         # keys in ascending order, duplicates included

All duplicate keys are kept: after add(10) twice, the set contains two 10s. An empty set has length 0, iterating over it yields an empty sequence, and no key is in it.

sl = SkipList(seed=7)
add 30, 10, 20, 10 in that order

list(sl) == [10, 10, 20, 30]
len(sl) == 4
(20 in sl) is True
(25 in sl) is False

Part 2 — Deletion and range queries

    def remove(self, key: int) -> bool: ...                      # remove ONE occurrence
    def keys_between(self, lo: int, hi: int) -> list[int]: ...   # every key with lo <= key <= hi

remove(key) removes one element equal to key and returns True; when there are several equal elements, it removes only one. If the key isn't in the set, it returns False and leaves the set unchanged.

keys_between(lo, hi) returns, in ascending order, every key with lo <= key <= hi, both ends inclusive; a duplicated key is returned as many times as it occurs. When lo > hi it returns an empty list. If it returns m keys, the expected time must be O(logn+m).

Continuing the example from Part 1, the set is now [10, 10, 20, 30]

sl.remove(10) is True            # now [10, 20, 30]
sl.remove(15) is False           # there is no 15, the set is unchanged
sl.keys_between(10, 25) == [10, 20]
sl.keys_between(20, 20) == [20]
sl.keys_between(31, 99) == []
sl.keys_between(25, 10) == []    # lo > hi

Part 3 — Order-statistic queries

class IndexedSkipList(SkipList):
    def kth(self, i: int) -> int: ...       # the i-th smallest key, counting from 0
    def rank(self, key: int) -> int: ...    # how many stored keys are strictly smaller than key

Add two operations to the structure from the first two parts (you can modify the original class directly, or write a subclass as above).

kth(i) returns the key at position i in ascending order, counting from 0, i.e. list(sl)[i]. If i is not in [0, len), raise IndexError; negative indices are also out of range, with no Python-style counting from the end.

rank(key) returns the number of elements in the set strictly smaller than key, counting each duplicate separately. key need not be in the set.

Both operations must run in expected O(logn) time, and add and remove must stay expected O(logn) as well. Counting nodes one by one along level 0 is O(n) and does not meet the requirement.

isl = IndexedSkipList(seed=7)
add 30, 10, 20, 10, 20, 5 in that order   # now [5, 10, 10, 20, 20, 30]
isl.remove(10) is True                    # now [5, 10, 20, 20, 30]

isl.kth(0) == 5      isl.kth(1) == 10      isl.kth(3) == 20      isl.kth(4) == 30
isl.kth(5)  -> IndexError
isl.kth(-1) -> IndexError

isl.rank(20) == 2        # the keys smaller than 20 are 5 and 10
isl.rank(21) == 4
isl.rank(5) == 0
isl.rank(1) == 0
isl.rank(99) == 5
solution:
Before you start, clarify three things. How duplicate keys are handled (all are kept, and remove deletes only one: this decides which node a deletion should unlink). Whether the complexity is worst-case or expected (expected, and over the structure's own random numbers, not over the input). What seed controls (only the internal shape; return values must not change with it: this is a property you can test directly).

A reasonable pace for 45 minutes: get Parts 1 and 2 written and running, and for Part 3 first explain what extra data to store and how updates change it, then write the code.

Part 1

Data layout. A node stores one key and an array next whose length equals its height; next[i] is its successor on level i. head has height MAX_LEVEL. We also keep _level: the number of levels actually in use, which is 1 for an empty list.

Invariants. The following three hold at the end of every operation; the check code verifies them from scratch after every operation:

  1. Level 0 strings all the nodes together in ascending key order (equal keys next to each other).
  2. Level i consists of exactly the nodes taller than i, in the same order as on level 0.
  3. _level equals the height of the tallest node (1 for an empty list), and head's pointers on level _level and above are all None.

Core subroutine. _predecessors(key) finds update[i] for each level i: the last node on level i whose key is strictly less than key, or head if there is none. The method is exactly the search from the statement: start at the top level, move right whenever you can, and when you can't, record the current node as this level's answer, drop down a level, and continue from the same node. Continuing from the same node works because its key is less than key and it is also on the next level down, so the answer on that level can't be to its left. When the walk ends, update[0].next[0] is the first node whose key is not less than key; lookup, insertion, deletion and range queries all start from there.

Insertion. Compute update, draw a height h, then on levels 0 .. h-1 link the new node in after update[i], which is ordinary linked-list insertion. When h exceeds _level, the predecessor on the newly used levels is head, which is what the update array is initialized to. Because the comparison is strict less-than, the new node is placed to the left of all existing equal keys. For a multiset any position would be correct, but deletion in Part 2 relies on "the node we operate on is always the leftmost of the equal keys".

Why the cost is expected O(logn). Let L=log1/p​n.

  • Number of pointers: a node has height at least k with probability pk−1, so the expected height is 1+p+p2+⋯=1/(1−p). With p=1/2 that is 2 pointers per node on average.
  • Number of levels: the expected number of nodes taller than L+c is n⋅pL+c=pc. So the probability of more than L+c levels is at most pc, and the expected number of levels is L+O(1).
  • Search steps: look at the search path backwards. Walking back from the end, when you are standing on some node on level i, if its height is greater than i+1, the path must have come down from the level above, so going backwards means "climb one level"; otherwise the path came from the left, so going backwards means "step one to the left". Whether its height exceeds i+1 is decided by one independent coin, with probability p. So each level climbed takes 1/p steps on average, and reaching level L takes L/p steps on average; above level L there are only a constant number of nodes in expectation. Pugh's original paper gives the result: the expected path length is at most L/p+1/(1−p), plus 1 for the number of comparisons.

With p=1/2 and n=8192 this bound is 2×13+2+1=29 comparisons. The check code inserts 8192 keys in ascending order (the order that turns an unbalanced binary search tree into a linked list) and does 2000 searches for each of 8 seeds: the mean number of comparisons is about 27, and the per-seed means range from 24 to 29. Note that the bound is on the expectation; one unlucky draw can exceed it.

MAX_LEVEL = 32 is more than enough for this problem's sizes: with p=1/2 a node draws 32 with probability 2−31, so over 2×105 insertions the probability that any node hits the cap is at most 2×105⋅2−31<10−4. Even if one does, only the height is truncated, and the structure is still correct.

import random

MAX_LEVEL = 32


class _Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "next")

    def __init__(self, key, height: int) -> None:
        self.key = key
        self.next = [None] * height       # next[i]: the following node on level i


class SkipList:
    """A sorted multiset. Level 0 links every node in key order; level i links the nodes taller than i."""

    def __init__(self, seed: int | None = None, p: float = 0.5) -> None:
        self._rng = random.Random(seed)   # the structure's own coins; they never change an answer
        self._p = p
        self._head = _Node(None, MAX_LEVEL)
        self._level = 1                   # number of levels in use
        self._n = 0

    def _random_height(self) -> int:
        h = 1
        while h < MAX_LEVEL and self._rng.random() < self._p:
            h += 1
        return h

    def _predecessors(self, key) -> list:
        """update[i] = the last node on level i whose key is < key (the head if there is none)."""
        update = [self._head] * MAX_LEVEL
        x = self._head
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            nxt = x.next[i]
            while nxt is not None and nxt.key < key:     # NOTE: strict <, so we stop left of equal keys
                x = nxt
                nxt = x.next[i]
            update[i] = x                 # the next level continues from the same node
        return update

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return self._n

    def __contains__(self, key) -> bool:
        x = self._predecessors(key)[0].next[0]           # the first node with key >= key, if any
        return x is not None and x.key == key

    def __iter__(self):
        x = self._head.next[0]
        while x is not None:
            yield x.key
            x = x.next[0]

    def add(self, key) -> None:
        update = self._predecessors(key)
        h = self._random_height()
        if h > self._level:
            self._level = h               # update[i] is already the head on the newly used levels
        node = _Node(key, h)
        for i in range(h):
            node.next[i] = update[i].next[i]
            update[i].next[i] = node
        self._n += 1

Part 2

Deletion. Compute update and let target = update[0].next[0]. If it doesn't exist or its key isn't key, the key is not in the set; return False. Otherwise target has to be unlinked from every level it is on.

The key point: for every i < height of target, update[i].next[i] is target. The reason: target is the first node in level-0 order whose key is not less than key; update[i] is the last node on level i whose key is less than key, so its successor on level i is "the first node on level i whose key is not less than key"; target is on level i and comes before all such nodes, so that successor is target. So unlinking on each level is the single statement update[i].next[i] = target.next[i].

This is also the easiest place to go wrong when there are duplicate keys. If the search stops as soon as it sees an equal key on a high level, it may get a tall equal node that is not the leftmost one; the update[i] on lower levels then points to another equal node to its left, and rewiring the pointers with the statement above drops the nodes between them from the list as well. The check code has a deliberately broken version written this way, and the random tests catch it.

After unlinking, if the top level has become empty, lower _level to keep invariant 3.

Range query. _predecessors(lo)[0].next[0] is the first node whose key is not less than lo; from there, walk right along level 0 until the key exceeds hi. Locating the start is expected O(logn), and after that each output key costs one step, for expected O(logn+m) in total. When lo > hi, the first node's key is already greater than hi, the loop doesn't run at all, and an empty list is returned, with no special case needed.

def remove(self, key) -> bool:
    update = self._predecessors(key)
    target = update[0].next[0]            # the LEFTMOST node with this key, if the key is present
    if target is None or target.key != key:
        return False
    for i in range(len(target.next)):
        update[i].next[i] = target.next[i]               # NOTE: update[i].next[i] is target on these levels
    while self._level > 1 and self._head.next[self._level - 1] is None:
        self._level -= 1                  # the tallest tower may just have gone
    self._n -= 1
    return True


def keys_between(self, lo, hi) -> list:
    out = []
    x = self._predecessors(lo)[0].next[0]
    while x is not None and x.key <= hi:
        out.append(x.key)
        x = x.next[0]
    return out


SkipList.remove = remove
SkipList.keys_between = keys_between

Part 3

What extra data to store. Give every pointer a span: how many level-0 positions that pointer jumps over in one step. Positions are numbered like this: head is 0, the i-th smallest key (counting from 0) is i + 1, and the None at the end is n + 1. The new invariant is:

  1. For every node x (including head) and every level i it uses, x.span[i] equals the position of x.next[i] minus the position of x.

Counting None as a position (n + 1) gives pointers to the end a well-defined span too, so insertion, deletion and queries need no special case for "there are no more nodes".

Position  0         1      2      3       4       5       6       7
Level 2   head ----------> 7 -----------------------------------> None      spans 2, 5
Level 1   head ----------> 7 -----------> 19 -------------------> None      spans 2, 2, 3
Level 0   head ---> 3 ---> 7 ---> 12 ---> 19 ---> 25 ---> 31 ---> None      all spans are 1

Queries. kth(i) has to reach position want = i + 1. Start at the top level and keep the current position in at; as long as at + span <= want, move right and add the span to at; otherwise drop down a level. Since the position of None, n + 1, is greater than want, the loop never runs off the end of the list. All spans on level 0 are 1, so at the end at == want. For kth(4) in the picture above: want = 5; level 2 moves to 7 (at = 2), level 1 moves to 19 (at = 4), level 0 moves to 25 (at = 5); return 25.

rank(key) is an ordinary search that adds up the spans it crosses along the way. The node it stops at is the last node whose key is less than key, and its position is exactly "the number of keys strictly less than key".

Updates. During the search, also record the position pos[i] of each level's predecessor. The new node's position is at = pos[0] + 1.

  • On levels i < h: the pointer update[i] → successor is cut into two by the new node. The span from update[i] to the new node is at - pos[i]. The old successor now has one more node in front of it, so its position becomes pos[i] + old span + 1, and the span from the new node to it is pos[i] + old span + 1 - at.
  • On levels h <= i < _level: the new node is not on this level, but it falls under the pointer from update[i], so that pointer's span increases by 1. This step is the easiest one to forget.
  • On newly used levels: first set head's span on these levels to n + 1 (pointing to None), then handle them as in the first case.

Deletion is the reverse: on the levels where target appears, the predecessor's span becomes "the sum of the two pieces minus 1"; on the levels above target, the span decreases by 1.

Cost. kth and rank follow a path of the same shape as an ordinary search: expected O(logn). add and remove now have to update every level in use, not just the h levels the new node is on; the expected number of levels is O(logn), so they are still expected O(logn). Memory-wise, each pointer gets one extra integer.

class _SpanNode(_Node):
    __slots__ = ("span",)

    def __init__(self, key, height: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(key, height)
        self.span = [1] * height          # span[i]: how many level-0 positions next[i] moves forward


class IndexedSkipList(SkipList):
    """Positions: the head is 0, the i-th smallest key is i + 1, the None at the end is n + 1.
    Invariant: x.span[i] == position(x.next[i]) - position(x) on every level in use."""

    def __init__(self, seed: int | None = None, p: float = 0.5) -> None:
        super().__init__(seed, p)
        self._head = _SpanNode(None, MAX_LEVEL)

    def _predecessors_with_pos(self, key) -> tuple[list, list[int]]:
        """As _predecessors, plus pos[i] = the position of update[i]."""
        update = [self._head] * MAX_LEVEL
        pos = [0] * MAX_LEVEL
        x, at = self._head, 0
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            nxt = x.next[i]
            while nxt is not None and nxt.key < key:
                at += x.span[i]
                x = nxt
                nxt = x.next[i]
            update[i], pos[i] = x, at
        return update, pos

    def add(self, key) -> None:
        update, pos = self._predecessors_with_pos(key)
        h = self._random_height()
        if h > self._level:
            for i in range(self._level, h):
                self._head.span[i] = self._n + 1         # a fresh level: head -> None
            self._level = h
        node = _SpanNode(key, h)
        at = pos[0] + 1                   # the new node's position
        for i in range(self._level):
            pred = update[i]
            if i < h:
                node.next[i] = pred.next[i]
                pred.next[i] = node
                node.span[i] = pos[i] + pred.span[i] + 1 - at    # the old target moved one place right
                pred.span[i] = at - pos[i]
            else:
                pred.span[i] += 1         # NOTE: the pointer passes over the new node -- easy to forget
        self._n += 1

    def remove(self, key) -> bool:
        update, _ = self._predecessors_with_pos(key)
        target = update[0].next[0]
        if target is None or target.key != key:
            return False
        h = len(target.next)
        for i in range(self._level):
            pred = update[i]
            if i < h:
                pred.span[i] += target.span[i] - 1       # two pointers merge, one position disappears
                pred.next[i] = target.next[i]
            else:
                pred.span[i] -= 1
        while self._level > 1 and self._head.next[self._level - 1] is None:
            self._level -= 1
        self._n -= 1
        return True

    def kth(self, i: int):
        if not 0 <= i < self._n:
            raise IndexError(f"index {i} out of range for {self._n} keys")
        x, at, want = self._head, 0, i + 1
        for lv in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            while at + x.span[lv] <= want:               # NOTE: None sits at n + 1 > want, so x never
                at += x.span[lv]                         #       runs off the end
                x = x.next[lv]
        return x.key

    def rank(self, key) -> int:
        return self._predecessors_with_pos(key)[1][0]    # position of the last node with a smaller key

Follow-ups

  • When is "a sorted array plus binary search" good enough? More often than you'd think. If the set never changes after it is built, a sorted array wins across the board: kth is a direct index, rank is one binary search, and memory is contiguous. With insertions and deletions, bisect.insort locates the spot in O(logn) and shifts elements in O(n), but the shift is a single memmove with a tiny constant. One measurement on CPython on this machine (the numbers will differ on other machines): inserting 20,000 random keys, insort is about twice as fast as the skip list above; the two break even at around 60,000; the version with spans is slower still, and at this problem's limit of 200,000 keys it is still no faster than insort. So in Python and at this scale, in an interview you should first say "I would use a sorted array", and then explain when it stops being enough: larger n with frequent updates (the total cost of all insort insertions is O(n2)), a language where pointer operations are cheap, or multiple threads modifying it concurrently.
  • What is the expectation in "expected O(logn)" taken over? What about the worst case? It is over the structure's own coins, with no assumption about the input, so inserting in ascending order does not degenerate the way an unbalanced binary search tree does. The worst case is still O(n): if every node draws height 1, it is a linked list, just with tiny probability. The probability of more than log2​n+c levels is at most 2−c; the check code counts the case n=1024, c=4 over 400 seeds, and about 6% of seeds exceed it, against a bound of 6.25%. The real weakness is an adversary who knows the random numbers: someone who can see the seed or observe the node heights can deliberately delete the tall nodes and make the structure degenerate. In that setting, use a deterministic balanced tree.
  • How do you choose p? It is a knob between memory and search time. The expected number of pointers per node is 1/(1−p): 2 for p=1/2 and 1.33 for p=1/4. The leading term of the search steps is (1/p)log1/p​n: 2log2​n for p=1/2 and 4log4​n=2log2​n for p=1/4, the same. So p=1/4 saves a third of the pointers without slowing searches down (the check code measures mean comparison counts of about 27 and 24.5 at n=8192), at the cost of more variance in the number of steps. With spans, every pointer also carries an extra integer, which makes a smaller p even more worthwhile. Redis's sorted sets use a skip list with spans, with p set to 1/4.
  • What do updates pay for the spans? Without spans, an insertion only touches the h levels the new node is on, 2 on average; with spans it has to update every level in use, about log1/p​n of them, and memory goes from about 120 bytes per key to about 200 (CPython, p=1/2; in a sorted array each key takes only one 8-byte pointer). Measured insertion is almost twice as slow. So only add spans when you actually need ranks. With rank, "how many keys are in the range" doesn't require listing the keys either: for integer keys the answer is max(0, rank(hi + 1) - rank(lo)), expected O(logn) regardless of how many keys are in the range. If every possible key is known in advance (offline, or a small value range), a Fenwick tree over the key range can also answer rank queries, and is shorter.
  • Compared with a balanced binary search tree, why would anyone choose a skip list? Both support the same set of operations at the same order of cost; the differences are in the guarantees and how hard they are to implement. Red-black trees and AVL trees give worst-case O(logn); a skip list gives an expectation. A skip list has no rotations; insertion and deletion only change a few predecessor pointers, so the code is much shorter and can be written in 45 minutes; level 0 is itself a sorted linked list, so range scans need no in-order traversal. Because modifications are local, it is also relatively easy to make concurrent (Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap is one). The cost is more pointers and scattered nodes, so its cache behavior is worse than arrays and B-trees.
Checks (runnable) 
import bisect
import math
import sys
import time


def _raises(exc, fn, *args):
    try:
        fn(*args)
    except exc:
        return True
    return False


def _filled(cls, keys, seed=7, p=0.5):
    sl = cls(seed=seed, p=p)
    for key in keys:
        sl.add(key)
    return sl


# --- the statement's examples for Parts 1 and 2, on both classes and under several seeds ---
assert len(SkipList()) == 0 and list(SkipList()) == [] and (5 in SkipList()) is False      # default arguments
for cls in (SkipList, IndexedSkipList):
    for seed in (0, 7, 12345):
        sl = _filled(cls, (30, 10, 20, 10), seed)
        assert list(sl) == [10, 10, 20, 30] and len(sl) == 4
        assert (20 in sl) is True and (25 in sl) is False
        assert sl.remove(10) is True and list(sl) == [10, 20, 30] and len(sl) == 3
        assert sl.remove(15) is False and list(sl) == [10, 20, 30] and len(sl) == 3
        assert sl.keys_between(10, 25) == [10, 20]
        assert sl.keys_between(20, 20) == [20]
        assert sl.keys_between(31, 99) == []
        assert sl.keys_between(25, 10) == []
        empty = cls(seed)
        assert len(empty) == 0 and list(empty) == [] and (5 in empty) is False
        assert empty.remove(5) is False and empty.keys_between(-10**9, 10**9) == []

    assert [isl.kth(i) for i in range(5)] == [5, 10, 20, 20, 30]
    assert _raises(IndexError, isl.kth, 5) and _raises(IndexError, isl.kth, -1)
    assert (isl.rank(20), isl.rank(21), isl.rank(5), isl.rank(1), isl.rank(99)) == (2, 4, 0, 0, 5)
    empty = IndexedSkipList(seed)
    assert empty.rank(3) == 0 and _raises(IndexError, empty.kth, 0)


# --- the two pictures on this page, rebuilt with the heights they show ---
def _with_heights(cls, keys, heights):
    sl = cls(seed=0)
    it = iter(heights)
    sl._random_height = lambda: next(it)             # choose the heights instead of flipping coins
    for key in keys:
        sl.add(key)
    return sl


def _level_nodes(sl, i):
    out = []
    x = sl._head.next[i]
    while x is not None:
        out.append(x)
        x = x.next[i]
    return out


def _comparisons(sl, key):
    """The walk of _predecessors, counted: (moves to the right, loop tests). Every loop test either moves
    right or ends a level, so tests = moves + levels."""
    moves = 0
    x = sl._head
    for i in range(sl._level - 1, -1, -1):
        while x.next[i] is not None and x.next[i].key < key:
            x = x.next[i]
            moves += 1
    return moves, moves + sl._level


PICTURE_KEYS = (3, 7, 12, 19, 25, 31)

assert pic._level == 3
assert [[x.key for x in _level_nodes(pic, i)] for i in (2, 1, 0)] == [[7], [7, 19], list(PICTURE_KEYS)]
assert [u.key for u in pic._predecessors(25)[:3]] == [19, 19, 7]     # levels 0, 1, 2
assert _comparisons(pic, 25)[0] == 2                                 # "2 steps to the right"
flat = _with_heights(SkipList, PICTURE_KEYS, (1,) * 6)               # level 0 only: a plain linked list
assert _comparisons(flat, 25)[0] == 4                                # "4 steps along level 0"

assert [x.span[2] for x in [head] + _level_nodes(pic, 2)] == [2, 5]
assert [x.span[1] for x in [head] + _level_nodes(pic, 1)] == [2, 2, 3]
assert [x.span[0] for x in [head] + _level_nodes(pic, 0)] == [1] * 7
assert pic.kth(4) == 25 and pic.rank(25) == 4


# --- invariants 1-4 of the explanation, checked from scratch against a sorted Python list ---
def _check_invariants(sl, model):
    nodes = _level_nodes(sl, 0)
    assert [x.key for x in nodes] == model and len(sl) == len(model)          # 1: level 0 holds every key
    tallest = max((len(x.next) for x in nodes), default=1)
    assert sl._level == tallest <= MAX_LEVEL                                  # 3: _level is the tallest tower
    assert all(sl._head.next[i] is None for i in range(sl._level, MAX_LEVEL))
    position = {id(x): i + 1 for i, x in enumerate(nodes)}
    position[id(sl._head)] = 0
    indexed = isinstance(sl, IndexedSkipList)
    for i in range(sl._level):
        want = [x for x in nodes if len(x.next) > i]                          # 2: level i = towers taller than i
        got = _level_nodes(sl, i)
        assert len(got) == len(want) and all(a is b for a, b in zip(got, want))
        if indexed:                                                           # 4: spans are position differences
            for x, nxt in zip([sl._head] + got, got + [None]):
                target = len(nodes) + 1 if nxt is None else position[id(nxt)]
                assert x.span[i] == target - position[id(x)]


def _run_random(cls, seed, n_ops, key_range, p=0.5, check_every=1):
    """A random operation sequence against the brute-force model: a sorted list scanned linearly."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    sl = cls(seed=seed * 7 + 1, p=p)
    model = []
    indexed = issubclass(cls, IndexedSkipList)
    for step in range(n_ops):
        r = rng.random()
        key = rng.randint(-key_range, key_range)
        if r < 0.40:
            sl.add(key)
            bisect.insort(model, key)
        elif r < 0.65:
            if model and rng.random() < 0.5:
                key = rng.choice(model)                  # half of the removals are guaranteed to hit
            present = key in model
            assert sl.remove(key) is present
            if present:
                model.remove(key)
        elif r < 0.75:
            assert (key in sl) is (key in model)
        elif r < 0.87:
            hi = key + rng.randint(-2, 12) * max(1, key_range // 8)
            want = [k for k in model if key <= k <= hi]
            assert sl.keys_between(key, hi) == want
            if indexed:                                  # the counting formula from the follow-ups
                assert max(0, sl.rank(hi + 1) - sl.rank(key)) == len(want)
        elif indexed and r < 0.94:
            assert sl.rank(key) == sum(k < key for k in model)
        elif indexed:
            i = rng.randint(-2, len(model) + 1)
            if 0 <= i < len(model):
                assert sl.kth(i) == model[i]
            else:
                assert _raises(IndexError, sl.kth, i)
        else:
            assert len(sl) == len(model) and (not model or (model[0] in sl and model[-1] in sl))
        if step % check_every == 0:
            _check_invariants(sl, model)
    _check_invariants(sl, model)
    assert list(sl) == model
    return len(model)


for cls in (SkipList, IndexedSkipList):
    for seed in range(40):
        _run_random(cls, seed, 400, 12)                  # few distinct keys: duplicates everywhere
    for seed in range(10):
        _run_random(cls, 100 + seed, 400, 10**9)         # the full key range
    for p in (0.25, 0.9, 1.0):                           # p = 1.0 is outside the contract: every tower hits
        for seed in range(5):                            # MAX_LEVEL, which exercises the cap
            _run_random(cls, 200 + seed, 300, 12, p=p)
    assert _run_random(cls, 300, 4000, 50) > 300         # one long run, invariants after EVERY operation
    assert _run_random(cls, 301, 30000, 10**9, check_every=500) > 3000
    assert _run_random(cls, 302, 30000, 400, check_every=500) > 3000


# --- negative controls: the two mistakes the explanation warns about must be caught by the tests above ---
class _ForgetsToWiden(IndexedSkipList):
    def add(self, key):
        update, pos = self._predecessors_with_pos(key)
        h = self._random_height()
        if h > self._level:
            for i in range(self._level, h):
                self._head.span[i] = self._n + 1
            self._level = h
        node = _SpanNode(key, h)
        at = pos[0] + 1
        for i in range(h):                               # BUG: the levels above h never get their += 1
            pred = update[i]
            node.next[i] = pred.next[i]
            pred.next[i] = node
            node.span[i] = pos[i] + pred.span[i] + 1 - at
            pred.span[i] = at - pos[i]
        self._n += 1


class _RemovesAnyEqualNode(SkipList):
    def remove(self, key):
        update = [self._head] * MAX_LEVEL
        x, target = self._head, None
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            while x.next[i] is not None and x.next[i].key < key:
                x = x.next[i]
            update[i] = x
            if target is None and x.next[i] is not None and x.next[i].key == key:
                target = x.next[i]                       # BUG: the first equal node seen from above is the
        if target is None:                               #      tallest-leftmost, not the leftmost
            return False
        for i in range(len(target.next)):
            update[i].next[i] = target.next[i]
        while self._level > 1 and self._head.next[self._level - 1] is None:
            self._level -= 1
        self._n -= 1
        return True


for broken in (_ForgetsToWiden, _RemovesAnyEqualNode):
    assert all(_raises(AssertionError, _run_random, broken, seed, 400, 12) for seed in range(5)), broken


# --- the seed changes the shape, never an answer ---
def _transcript(seed, p):
    rng = random.Random(99)                              # the same operations every time
    sl = IndexedSkipList(seed=seed, p=p)
    out = []
    for _ in range(1500):
        r, key = rng.random(), rng.randint(-30, 30)
        if r < 0.45:
            sl.add(key)
        elif r < 0.70:
            out.append(sl.remove(key))
        elif r < 0.80:
            out.append(key in sl)
        elif r < 0.90:
            out.append(sl.keys_between(key, key + 9))
        else:
            out.append((len(sl), sl.rank(key), sl.kth(len(sl) // 2) if len(sl) else None))
    out.append(list(sl))
    return out, sl._level

# --- the cost claims of Part 1, across 8 seeds: pointers per node and comparisons per search ---
N_COST = 8192
measured = {}
for p in (0.5, 0.25):
    levels_needed = math.log(N_COST, 1 / p)
    bound = levels_needed / p + 1 / (1 - p) + 1          # Pugh's bound on the expected number of comparisons
    means = []
    for seed in range(8):
        sl = _filled(SkipList, range(N_COST), seed, p)   # ascending: the order that ruins a plain BST
        pointers = sum(len(x.next) for x in _level_nodes(sl, 0)) / N_COST
        assert abs(pointers - 1 / (1 - p)) < 0.03 / (1 - p)          # within 3% of 1 / (1 - p)
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        mean = sum(_comparisons(sl, rng.randrange(N_COST))[1] for _ in range(2000)) / 2000
        assert mean < 1.2 * bound                        # one unlucky seed may exceed an EXPECTATION a little
        means.append(mean)
    measured[p] = (bound, sum(means) / len(means), min(means), max(means))
    assert measured[p][1] <= bound                       # ... but the average over seeds does not

# --- timing (follow-ups): printed, not asserted, because wall-clock time on a shared machine is noisy ---
def _best_of_three(fn):
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(3):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - start)
    return best
